Training and Comparing ML Classifiers on IMDb Reviews

Author

Felix Lennert

Published

February 10, 2026

Description and motivation

I taught a graduate Computational Social Science course at Leipzig University that focused heavily on quantitative text analysis. Inevitably, students asked a very practical question: given limited time and compute, which supervised text classification approach should we choose? In this report, I therefore compare four families of models for sentiment classification of IMDb movie reviews: a dictionary-based method, several bag-of-words classifiers, a fine-tuned BERT model, and a zero-shot local LLM. Using a fixed budget of 500 labeled training examples for all trained models, I document how preprocessing and model choice affect accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and runtime—and what I would recommend in different real-world scenarios.

Data source

The analysis uses IMDb movie reviews with binary sentiment labels (positive/negative) from Kaggle, a widely used benchmark in sentiment analysis. The data are pre-labeled, reasonably balanced across classes, and contain long-form, naturalistic text—making them well suited to comparing shallow and deep text classifiers on the same task. For copyright reasons, the data themselves are not published here; the code below assumes the CSV lives in files_for_project_backlog/ml_classifiers/imdb-reviews.csv.

Outline

The workflow is as follows:

  1. Load and split the data: 500 reviews for training (stratified by sentiment), the remainder as a held-out test set.
  2. Preprocess text: tokenize, remove stop words, optionally stem (for the dictionary method), filter to the 1,000 most frequent tokens, and create TF–IDF features (with additional normalization for SVM).
  3. Train and evaluate models:
    • Dictionary-based sentiment scores using AFINN.
    • Bag-of-words models: Naive Bayes, logistic regression, Lasso, Ridge, linear SVM, random forest, and XGBoost.
    • Fine-tuned BERT (bert-base-uncased).
    • Zero-shot local LLM classification using Qwen 2.5 3B via Ollama.
  4. Compare results: summarize performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) and runtime across all approaches, and interpret the trade-offs.
  5. (Optional) Tune models: use cross-validation to optimize hyperparameters (e.g., regularization strength for Lasso/Ridge, number of tokens, tree depth) and adjust BERT training settings (epochs, learning rate, max sequence length) or LLM prompts for further gains.

Analysis

Setup and data split

Show code 
needs(tidyverse, tidytext, textrecipes, tidymodels, workflows, yardstick, discrim,
      naivebayes, SnowballC, stopwords, textdata, tictoc, jsonlite,
      glmnet, LiblineaR, ranger, xgboost, here, reticulate)

base <- here("files_for_project_backlog", "ml_classifiers")
imdb_raw <- read_csv(here(base, "imdb-reviews.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  rename(text = review)

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(imdb_raw, prop = 500 / nrow(imdb_raw), strata = sentiment)
imdb_train <- training(split)
imdb_test <- testing(split)

imdb_train |> write_csv(here(base, "train_split.csv"))
imdb_test |> write_csv(here(base, "test_split.csv"))

Recipes

Show code 
recipe_bow <- recipe(sentiment ~ text, data = imdb_train) |>
  step_tokenize(text) |>
  step_tokenfilter(text, max_tokens = 1000) |>
  step_tfidf(text)

recipe_svm <- recipe(sentiment ~ text, data = imdb_train) |>
  step_tokenize(text) |>
  step_tokenfilter(text, max_tokens = 1000) |>
  step_tfidf(text) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

run_bow <- function(name, wf, label_tic = name) {
  tic(label_tic)
  fit_wf <- fit(wf, data = imdb_train)
  pred <- augment(fit_wf, imdb_test)
  end_time <- toc(quiet = TRUE)
  elapsed <- end_time$toc-end_time$tic
  pred |>
    mutate(sentiment = factor(sentiment, levels = c("negative", "positive"))) |> 
    metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, f_meas)(
      truth = sentiment,
      estimate = .pred_class
    ) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) |>
    mutate(classifier = name, runtime_seconds = round(elapsed, 2), .before = 1) |>
    rename(f1 = f_meas) |>
    select(classifier, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, runtime_seconds)
}

Dictionary (AFINN)

As a minimal baseline, I first use a dictionary-based classifier. Reviews are tokenized and stemmed, then matched against the AFINN sentiment lexicon. For each review, I compute the mean sentiment score across all matched tokens and classify it as positive if the score is greater than zero and negative otherwise. This method is fast and transparent but intentionally ignores word order and context.

Show code 
tic("Dictionary (AFINN)")
afinn_stemmed <- get_sentiments("afinn") |>
  mutate(stemmed = wordStem(word, language = "en"))
scored <- imdb_test |>
  rowid_to_column("doc") |>
  unnest_tokens(token, text) |>
  anti_join(get_stopwords(), by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  mutate(stemmed = wordStem(token, language = "en")) |>
  inner_join(afinn_stemmed, by = "stemmed", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(doc) |>
  summarise(sentiment_score = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(
    .pred_class = if_else(sentiment_score > 0, "positive", "negative"),
    .pred_class = factor(.pred_class, levels = c("positive", "negative"))
  )
imdb_afinn <- imdb_test |>
  rowid_to_column("doc") |>
  select(doc, sentiment) |>
  mutate(sentiment = factor(sentiment, levels = c("positive", "negative"))) |>
  left_join(select(scored, doc, .pred_class), by = "doc") |>
  mutate(
    .pred_class = replace_na(as.character(.pred_class), "positive"),
    .pred_class = factor(.pred_class, levels = c("positive", "negative"))
  )
dict_time <- toc(quiet = TRUE)
elapsed <- dict_time$toc-dict_time$tic
dict_metrics <- imdb_afinn |>
  metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, f_meas)(
    truth = sentiment,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) |>
  mutate(classifier = "Dictionary (AFINN)", runtime_seconds = round(elapsed, 2), .before = 1) |>
  rename(f1 = f_meas) |>
  select(classifier, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, runtime_seconds)

Bag-of-words models

Next, I apply a family of supervised models to the same TF–IDF representation of the reviews (with an additional normalization step for SVM). These models keep the simplicity and speed of the bag-of-words assumption but use more flexible decision rules: from Naive Bayes and (penalized) logistic regression to linear SVMs and tree-based ensembles (random forest, XGBoost). All models are trained on exactly the same 500 labeled examples to make their comparison fair.

Show code 
wf_nb <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  naive_Bayes() |> set_engine("naivebayes") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_glm <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_lasso <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_ridge <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  logistic_reg(penalty = 0.01, mixture = 0) |> set_engine("glmnet") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_svm <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_svm) |> add_model(
  svm_linear() |> set_engine("LiblineaR") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_rf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  rand_forest(trees = 100) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("classification")
)
wf_xgb <- workflow() |> add_recipe(recipe_bow) |> add_model(
  boost_tree(trees = 50) |> set_engine("xgboost") |> set_mode("classification")
)

bow_metrics <- bind_rows(
  run_bow("Naive Bayes (TF-IDF)", wf_nb),
  run_bow("Logistic regression (glm)", wf_glm),
  run_bow("Lasso (glmnet)", wf_lasso),
  run_bow("Ridge (glmnet)", wf_ridge),
  run_bow("SVM linear (LiblineaR)", wf_svm),
  run_bow("Random forest (ranger)", wf_rf),
  run_bow("XGBoost", wf_xgb)
)

BERT (Python via reticulate)

Fine-tuned bert-base-uncased on 500 samples. Writes metrics to bert_results.json for the R chunk below.

Show code 
# Use reticulate to call the BERT training script in the bert-env conda environment.
use_condaenv("bert-env", required = TRUE)
source_python(here(base, "run_bert.py"))

# run_bert.py defines main() which trains BERT and writes bert_results.json
main()

BERT metrics and LLM zero-shot

Show code 
bert_metrics <- jsonlite::read_json(here(base, "bert_results.json")) |>
  as.list() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(classifier = "BERT (fine-tuned)", .before = 1)

needs(ellmer, ollamar)
n_gpt <- 100
imdb_test_gpt <- imdb_test |> slice_head(n = n_gpt)
sentiment_type <- ellmer::type_object(
  sentiment = ellmer::type_enum("Sentiment", values = c("positive", "negative"))
)
prompt <- "You are a movie expert. Classify the review as positive or negative. Reply with one word: positive or negative."

tic("LLM zero-shot")
gpt_preds <- map(imdb_test_gpt$text, function(txt) {
  ch <- ellmer::chat_ollama(model = "qwen2.5:3b", system_prompt = prompt,
    params = ellmer::params(temperature = 0.1, seed = 42))
  as.character(ch$chat_structured(txt, type = sentiment_type)$sentiment)
}, .progress = TRUE)

gpt_time <- toc(quiet = TRUE)
gpt_elapsed <- gpt_time$toc-gpt_time$tic

gpt_df <- imdb_test_gpt |>
  select(sentiment) |>
  mutate(
    .pred_class = factor(unlist(gpt_preds), levels = c("positive", "negative")),
    sentiment = factor(sentiment, levels = c("positive", "negative"))
  )
gpt_metrics <- gpt_df |>
  metric_set(accuracy, precision, recall, f_meas)(
    truth = sentiment,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    event_level = "second"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) |>
  mutate(
    classifier = paste0("LLM zero-shot (n=", n_gpt, ")"),
    runtime_seconds = round(gpt_elapsed, 2),
    .before = 1
  ) |>
  rename(f1 = f_meas) |>
  select(classifier, accuracy, precision, recall, f1, runtime_seconds)

Conclusions

Stemming and token filtering improve dictionary and bag-of-words baselines. With 500 examples, TF-IDF + penalized regression or tree models outperform the dictionary; BERT reaches highest accuracy at higher compute cost. The zero-shot LLM (Qwen 2.5 3B) performs well without training and is flexible—change the prompt instead of retraining. In a more production-like setting, additional tuning steps would be natural: grid-searching penalties and token thresholds for bag-of-words models, adjusting BERT epochs and learning rates, or iterating on prompt design and few-shot examples for the LLM. As a rule of thumb, use dictionary or Naive Bayes for very quick baselines, tuned penalized/logit or tree models when you need strong performance on limited compute, BERT when you have labels and GPU time, and LLM prompting when labels are scarce or categories change frequently.
